Massachusetts Judge Throws Out DOJ Bid for Harvard Admissions Data
stories.ltme_summary: A federal judge in Massachusetts has dismissed the US Department of Justice's lawsuit seeking to make Harvard University produce applicant-level admissions records. The DOJ sought the data in an investigation into whether Harvard kept using race-conscious admissions after the 2023 Students for Fair Admissions decision. The dismissal leaves the underlying allegations unresolved. Legal Tech Monitor frames the ruling as a procedural win relevant to discovery and data governance.
stories.hook: Massachusetts judge dismisses DOJ bid to force Harvard to hand over applicant-level admissions data

Lawyers’ AI use doesn’t justify slashing $115K fee award, appellate court says
stories.ltme_summary: According to Reuters, the US 10th Circuit Court of Appeals upheld a $115,000 fee award to Brownstein Hyatt Farber Schreck, defence counsel in a trade secrets dispute brought by Flux Drive. The panel said plaintiffs had not shown that the use of AI made the hours actually worked unreasonable. The court also upheld dismissal of the lawsuit. Judge Carolyn McHugh wrote the unanimous opinion, stressing that lawyers must still verify authorities themselves.
stories.hook: Tenth Circuit upholds $115,000 fee award despite Flux Drive's claim that defence AI use should cut the bill

stories.title: Judiciary efforts to create rules for AI stalling amid concerns
stories.ltme_summary: The ABA Journal, citing a Law360 story, reports that efforts to write rules on artificial intelligence use in US federal courts have stalled. The Advisory Committee on Evidence Rules, which advises the Judicial Conference, has faced setbacks and resistance, including criticism of a proposed rule on AI deepfakes. Maura R. Grossman, a University of Waterloo professor whose research shaped the proposals, told Law360 she was not hopeful.
stories.hook: Federal judiciary's AI evidence rules stall as lawyers and judges criticise the deepfake proposal
entities: Judicial Conference of the United States

Gibson Dunn Could Roll Out The Welcome Mat For Up To 120 Weil Lawyers
stories.ltme_summary: Above the Law, citing the Financial Times, reports that Gibson Dunn is in talks to hire as many as 120 Weil lawyers across the US and London, including more than 20 partners. The group includes Andrew Chizzik, head of Weil's New York private funds practice, and James Bromley and James Sargent, London co-heads. Weil is preparing to wind down after partner departures and failed merger talks. Neither firm commented.
stories.hook: Gibson Dunn in talks to hire up to 120 Weil lawyers as Weil moves towards dissolution

stories.title: Former Weil Partners Lawyer Up As The Firm’s Wind-Down Turns Into A Fight Over What’s Left
stories.ltme_summary: Above the Law, citing the Financial Times, reports that a group of about 10 former Weil Gotshal partners has hired Peter Wang, a Foley & Lardner litigator, over the firm's wind-down. The group is said to be probing whether there was a breach of fiduciary duty by Weil's leadership. Separately, Ramona Nee is reported to be moving to Kirkland & Ellis with a team, with Bloomberg Law and Law.com giving differing headcounts.
stories.hook: Former Weil partners hire Foley & Lardner's Peter Wang as Weil's wind-down raises fiduciary duty questions

stories.title: Intellectual Property Office gets new weapons to protect design
stories.ltme_summary: The government has announced changes to UK design law, after a 2025 IPO consultation found that resolving design disputes falls heavily on small firms, some spending £10,000 to £50,000. Proposals include IPO powers to check novelty and refuse bad-faith applications, a route for registered design cases in the IPEC Small Claims Track, a 30-month deferment period and wider unregistered design protection. Legislation will follow when parliamentary time allows.
stories.hook: UK government plans IPO powers to refuse bad-faith design filings and a small claims route for design disputes

stories.title: 'Sycophantic' AI inflaming litigants in person, digital justice expert claims
stories.ltme_summary: The Law Society Gazette reports that Dr Natalie Byrom, in a report for the Nuffield Family Justice Observatory, warns that sycophantic AI advice tools are misleading litigants in person in family courts. She urges the MoJ and HMCTS to assess vendor lock-in and sovereignty risks, reduce reliance on a small number of foreign AI developers, and consider registration rather than reserved activity for AI advice tools. The report criticises a delegation-by-default approach.
stories.hook: Natalie Byrom warns that sycophantic AI is misleading litigants in person and urges MoJ to cut vendor dependence

Trial opens for suspect whose multiple email threats include ‘skinning’ federal judge
stories.ltme_summary: Opening statements were made in the trial of David Brooks Pokorny, 45, of El Cerrito, California, who is charged with making felony threats against a judicial officer. Prosecutor Kent Stejskal told the jury that 11 emails sent in 44 minutes to assault, kidnap and murder Judge Charles Breyer were true threats. The defence argues the emails are protected free speech. Judge Jon Tigar is presiding.
stories.hook: Trial opens in Northern District of California over emails threatening to kill Judge Charles Breyer

stories.title: AI Connectors For E-Discovery: Great To Drive, But There Are Speed Limits
stories.ltme_summary: A columnist for Above the Law warns that Reveal's Onna platform can now collect conversations employees generate in Claude Enterprise, following earlier support for ChatGPT and Gemini. The column argues that prompts and AI outputs may be discoverable and urges in-house teams to train staff on the risk. It is commentary on e-discovery tooling and employee AI use.
stories.hook: Reveal's Onna can now collect employees' Claude Enterprise chats, making AI prompts discoverable

stories.title: AI May Speed Up Legal Research, But That Doesn’t Automatically Shrink The Bill
stories.ltme_summary: The Tenth Circuit panel, in an opinion by Judge Carolyn McHugh, affirmed a $114,663.11 fee award to Brownstein Hyatt Farber Schreck after Flux Drive's trade secrets suit was dismissed. Flux Drive had argued the firm's use of AI and online research tools should have cut its fees, but the court said it pointed to no specific inflated billing entry. The panel noted AI may reduce research time while lawyers must still verify their authorities.
stories.hook: Tenth Circuit upholds $114,663.11 fee award to Brownstein Hyatt despite AI-reduction argument
